The zero coupon limits cash interest on that specific issuance, but the consolidated interest line and project financing still need watching. Nor should a share-price forecast turn a large contracted-rent number into today's equity value without accounting for debt, construction spend and the timing of deliveries.

The $9.1 billion lease is a schedule, not Q4 sales

Cipher said the expanded Barber Lake lease has approximately $9.1 billion of contracted revenue over a 20-year term, including about $5.2 billion added in the amendment. The amendment was disclosed in a September 24 filing; repeating the total today does not make the contract itself a new November 2 signing. Dividing $9.1 billion by 20 yields $455 million per year as a simple lifetime average, or $113.75 million per quarter. That average is not the contractual quarterly payment schedule, a 2027 revenue forecast or near-term free cash flow. Cipher says deliveries are phased to the tenant's compute deployment, and the Q3 HPC revenue came from Black Pearl, a different campus.

The actual progression matters more than the headline total. At Black Pearl, rent began when capacity was delivered, and the company says additional halls there and at Barber Lake are scheduled to come online in phases through year-end. Each energized, accepted hall can change recognized rent. A delayed hall can postpone it. The next report needs to show the number of delivered halls or capacity, recognized HPC rent, project operating expense, and whether new debt or equity was needed to finish delivery. Without those pieces, a large multiyear agreement cannot be converted responsibly into a near-term stock price target.

Power rights and financing decide the 2027 branch

Cipher describes a roughly 5.9-gigawatt development pipeline. That is not the same thing as 5.9 gigawatts of energized, leased data centers. In the November 2 update, it reported conditional ERCOT classifications for 1 gigawatt at Colchis and an additional 1.6 gigawatts of studied load with provisional controllable-load designations. It has also begun lateral natural-gas pipeline development that it says could support up to 2.5 gigawatts of on-site generation. These are development steps with regulatory, construction, fuel-supply and financing conditions, not operating megawatts.

The company also identifies 270 megawatts potentially available in 2027 while it advances tenant discussions and design work. Available capacity is not a signed tenant. A bullish 2027 case requires timely power approvals, contracts, construction and rent commencement at attractive project economics. A base case would show steady rent growth but continued consolidated losses while the portfolio is built. A bearish case would see power or tenant delays combine with construction costs or financing pressure. These are conditional paths, not precise share-price forecasts; the disclosed inputs do not justify an honest dollar target today.

This makes dilution and capital structure part of the same forecast. The Q3 balance sheet lists 415.093 million common shares outstanding at September 30, versus 404.963 million at the end of 2025, a 2.5% increase. It also lists $5.447 billion of long-term borrowings and $0.656 billion of cash and equivalents, alongside $1.719 billion of restricted cash. Restricted cash is not interchangeable with freely available cash. Project-level debt may be supported by future rent, but common shareholders still need a clear bridge from completed campuses to cash after interest, maintenance and reinvestment.

What would change the CIFR forecast

The encouraging evidence is tangible: a first $5.852 million rent line, a low direct-cost line at this early stage and more capacity scheduled for delivery. TECHi’s CIFR quote page and forecast page provide dated market and analyst context, which should be kept separate from this filing-based operating test. The counterargument is equally tangible: mining sales fell 70.9% year over year, Q3 operating loss widened to $71.9 million, and reported net income benefited from a warrant revaluation rather than operating profit. The market's early decline does not settle which side wins over 2027. It signals that investors are demanding proof beyond the size of signed contracts.

For a constructive revision, watch for quarterly HPC rent rising toward the $17.3 million static adjusted-EBITDA hurdle and, over a longer period, for the operating-loss bridge to narrow without an equal jump in debt or shares. Those levels are TECHi sensitivities based on Q3 inputs, not company targets. A flat or falling rent line after promised hall deliveries, higher direct costs, weaker project margins or another delay in firm power access would weaken the thesis. An improving GAAP operating result together with cash generation would matter more than an isolated positive net-income print.

What to watch

The next dated test is Cipher's fourth-quarter 2026 results, expected in the next earnings cycle; the company has not provided a confirmed release date in this November 2 update. Before then, watch for disclosures on year-end data-hall delivery, ERCOT's final treatment of conditional load, and new tenant agreements for the 270 megawatts it identifies for 2027. The practical question for CIFR is whether each new megawatt becomes recognized rent and cash quickly enough to outrun the cost of building it.

data.title: Advantest vs Tokyo Electron: 9.1% slide leaves a 31% valuation premium
data.description:
Advantest fell 9.1% and Tokyo Electron dropped 7.5% in Thursday morning trading in Tokyo on November 5. At nearly simultaneous Yahoo Finance observations around 9:59 a.m. JST, the semiconductor equipment stocks traded at ¥31,420 and ¥8,940, respectively, against Wednesday's closes of ¥34,570 and ¥9,663.

The selloff leaves a revealing difference: Advantest costs about 30.6 times its company's forecast earnings for the year ending March 2027, versus 23.4 times for Tokyo Electron. That is a roughly 31% premium. Yet Tokyo Electron needs substantially faster second-half operating-profit growth to deliver its outlook. The choice is between two different execution risks, rather than two interchangeable ways to buy the AI investment cycle.

What the Tokyo selloff changed

The Advantest observation was timestamped 9:58:49 a.m. JST; the Tokyo Electron observation followed three seconds later. These are fixed, dated morning-session snapshots used at publication, in Japanese yen. They were already about 15 minutes old when retrieved; the provider's formal delay specification is unavailable. They are not closing prices or a claim of live quotations.

Those moves use the previous regular-session close as the denominator: ¥31,420 divided by ¥34,570, minus one, gives a 9.11% decline for Advantest. The equivalent Tokyo Electron calculation gives a 7.48% decline. Merely returning to those closes would require gains of about 10.0% and 8.1% from the observed prices, before transaction costs. A large fall does not make the recovery mathematically symmetrical.

The market observations establish the selling, but do not identify one definitive cause. Nor do they establish that either company's earnings forecast has changed. Advantest's guidance used here was released October 28; Tokyo Electron's was released October 30. This comparison applies those dated forecasts to a new market development. It does not present the financial releases as Thursday announcements.

A 31% premium, with two important qualifications

Advantest's October 28 forecast puts annual basic earnings per share at ¥1,027.08. Tokyo Electron's October 30 financial release forecasts ¥381.69. Dividing the observed share prices by those figures produces 30.59 and 23.42 times earnings. Dividing the first multiple by the second, then subtracting one, produces the 30.6% premium.

Both forecasts cover April 1, 2026, through March 31, 2027. Advantest calls that fiscal 2026; Tokyo Electron calls it fiscal 2027. Comparing the fiscal labels without the actual dates would put an unnecessary obstacle in front of an otherwise matched-period calculation. These are company-guidance multiples, rather than analyst-consensus or next-twelve-month estimates.

The accounting is less perfectly matched. Advantest reports under IFRS and Tokyo Electron under Japanese GAAP. Their company EPS figures are useful published benchmarks, but do not become a standardized measure of recurring operating earnings merely because they cover the same period. This is an equity-price comparison, not an enterprise-value calculation adjusted for every balance-sheet asset and liability.

Tokyo Electron also completed a five-for-one share split on October 1. Its forecast EPS is explicitly adjusted for that split, matching the post-split price. Comparing ¥8,940 directly with Advantest's ¥31,420 would say nothing useful about which business is cheaper: nominal share prices depend on how many shares divide the ownership.

Advantest has the smaller profit step, but a margin retreat

Advantest's forecast calls for ¥1,863 billion of annual revenue and ¥967 billion of operating profit. Against first-half revenue of ¥845.2 billion and operating profit of ¥456.8 billion, the company projects ¥1,017.8 billion and ¥510.2 billion, respectively, in the second half. The implied sequential operating-profit increase is 11.7% using the company's rounded figures.

That increase comes with a lower operating margin: 50.1% in the second half versus 54.0% in the first. Revenue growth can therefore exceed profit growth without signaling a missed forecast. An investor who extrapolates the first-half margin through March would be assuming something stronger than management's published outlook.

The spending assumptions help explain the hurdle. Advantest budgets ¥69.1 billion of research and development in the second half, against ¥44.9 billion in the first, and ¥37 billion of capital expenditure versus ¥23 billion. Research expenditure affects operating earnings; capital spending affects cash and future depreciation under the applicable accounting. They should not be subtracted from profit in the same way.

Advantest attributes tester demand to increasing volumes and complexity of high-performance AI semiconductors, including advanced packaging. Its half-year results also describe efforts to expand production capacity across the supply chain. Those are reasons its earnings might remain resilient, but meeting customer demand still depends on equipment delivery and component availability. A favorable end market is not the same as completed revenue.

Tokyo Electron's discount comes with a steeper delivery requirement

Tokyo Electron forecasts ¥3,700 billion in annual sales and ¥1,169 billion in operating income. Its first-half release reports ¥1,667.455 billion and ¥506.776 billion. Subtracting those actual results leaves ¥2,032.545 billion of sales and ¥662.224 billion of operating income to be delivered from October through March.

That means second-half sales need to rise about 21.9% from the first half, while operating income needs to rise 30.7%. The implied operating margin is approximately 32.6%, versus 30.4% in the first half. Unlike Advantest, Tokyo Electron needs both a larger revenue base and a higher margin to reach its full-year operating target.

This is why the lower multiple cannot settle the comparison. Tokyo Electron offers a less expensive claim on the earnings it forecasts, but a larger portion of the annual operating result still lies ahead. Shipment timing, customer acceptance, product mix and spending discipline can all affect whether revenue growth produces the required profit growth. The calculations describe the hurdle; they do not establish that management will miss it.

TECHi's earlier Tokyo Electron analysis examined that profit requirement during the November 2 rally. Thursday's new issue is relative valuation after a sharp decline in both stocks. Tokyo Electron could close part of the valuation gap by delivering its forecast while Advantest loses some of its premium. It could also remain cheaper because investors demand compensation for the larger execution step.

Earnings quality and cash complicate the apparent winner

Advantest's first-half net income was ¥368.1 billion, but its release identifies approximately ¥57 billion of financial income, primarily valuation gains on investment securities. That income is outside operating profit. It is not equivalent to cash earned by selling more testers, and its future contribution depends in part on investment values.

The premium comparison therefore deserves extra caution: a headline EPS multiple can look more attractive when non-operating gains boost the earnings denominator. The release does not provide a directly comparable, tax-adjusted recurring EPS measure for both companies. Removing the entire ¥57 billion from net income would mix pre-tax and after-tax quantities, so this comparison does not manufacture an adjusted multiple.

At September 30, Advantest reported ¥401.785 billion of cash and cash equivalents, ¥89.486 billion of bonds and ¥17.760 billion of current and non-current lease liabilities. Tokyo Electron reported ¥578.601 billion of cash and cash equivalents; its balance sheet does not separately list a bank-borrowing or bond line. That absence should not be expanded into a claim that every form of financing obligation is zero.

The cash figures also are not an argument for subtracting one company's total cash from its share price. They are historical company-wide balances, while the prices are per-share November observations. A proper cash-adjusted valuation would require matching outstanding shares, debt, leases and other relevant claims on the same basis. Here, the figures show liquidity context and the limits of using a simple P/E ranking.

What would change the forecast comparison?

If both companies achieve their current annual EPS forecasts and the observed valuation multiples hold, neither assumption by itself produces a gain from the snapshot prices: those prices already equal forecast EPS multiplied by the calculated multiples. A bullish forecast needs an additional argument for higher earnings, a higher valuation multiple, or both.

A useful stress test reverses the question. If annual EPS were 10% below each company's guidance while prices stayed unchanged, Advantest's multiple would rise to about 34.0 times and Tokyo Electron's to 26.0 times. Those are hypothetical denominator changes, calculated by dividing each current multiple by 0.9. They are neither revised forecasts nor estimates of the probability of a miss.

The strongest case for paying Advantest's premium is that tester demand tied to chip complexity proves more durable and its smaller second-half profit step leaves less execution distance. The strongest objection is that its forecast already embeds exceptionally high operating margins, while investment gains and exchange rates complicate the earnings base. A smaller hurdle is not an inexpensive hurdle.

Tokyo Electron's case improves if its shipments and margins deliver the required second-half acceleration without a corresponding valuation increase. The countercase is that lower valuation is compensation for a more demanding forecast, rather than a mispricing. Evidence of weaker profit conversion would strengthen that objection. Better operating delivery at both companies could support both stocks; their relative performance still depends on what investors pay for those earnings.

What to watch

The next dated market checkpoints are Tokyo's 11:30 a.m. JST morning close and 3:30 p.m. cash close on November 5, under the exchange's trading schedule. Those observations will show whether the early declines persist; they will not, on their own, validate or invalidate the March 2027 earnings forecasts. For the business comparison, watch subsequent company guidance and reported second-half revenue, operating margins and non-operating income. The decisive question is whether each company earns the profit its own valuation now asks investors to assume.

data.title: Sandisk stock forecast: Kioxia’s 11% Tokyo slide tests NAND growth
data.description:
Tokyo's first trading hour on Monday delivered a sharp warning to investors awaiting the next U.S. session in Sandisk. Kioxia Holdings, the Japanese flash-memory maker that supplies substantially all of Sandisk's flash wafers through their joint ventures, traded at ¥11,985 at 9:34 a.m. Japan time, down 11.0% from Friday's ¥13,470 close, according to a delayed Yahoo Finance quote. Sandisk shares had already fallen 13.4% in Friday's U.S. session on Alpaca's IEX closing series. Those are observations in two different markets and sessions, not a prediction that Sandisk will repeat Kioxia's Monday move.

The useful forecast question is narrower: does Kioxia's share-price slide signal that the pricing surge in flash memory has reached a plateau, or is Sandisk's more ambitious near-term revenue guide still credible? TECHi's calculation from the companies' published figures exposes the gap. Kioxia expects revenue to rise just 0.8% sequentially in its October–December quarter, from ¥2.480 trillion to ¥2.500 trillion. Sandisk guides to a 12.4% sequential increase at the midpoint of its next-quarter range, from $11.031 billion to $12.400 billion. The difference is 11.6 percentage points. It is a comparison of growth rates, not a conversion of yen into dollars or an assertion that the two companies sell the same product mix.

Why Kioxia's fall matters to Sandisk

The two companies are closer than ordinary semiconductor peers. Sandisk says in its latest Form 10-Q that it procures substantially all its flash-based memory wafers from three manufacturing ventures with Kioxia. The filing also describes facility arrangements, prepayments and research commitments tied to those ventures. They share a production base, although they do not have identical customers, sales channels or financial statements. A shift in wafer economics at one partner therefore deserves attention at the other; it does not mechanically transfer one company's stock return to the other.

The new signal is the market's first reaction after Kioxia's October 30 results. The Kioxia financial release reported September-quarter revenue of ¥2.480 trillion, up from ¥1.767 trillion in the June quarter. That is a 40.3% sequential increase, driven, the company said, by higher average selling prices, AI data-center demand and more bits shipped. Yet its next-quarter outlook is ¥2.500 trillion of revenue and ¥1.995 trillion of operating profit, essentially level with the latest quarter's ¥2.480 trillion and ¥1.995 trillion. Kioxia says strong data-center demand should continue, while exchange rates could weigh on the next three months. Flat guidance after exceptional growth is not the same as collapsing demand. It does, however, change the incremental growth question investors must answer.

Sandisk's October 29 earnings release shows a different trajectory. Revenue grew 23% sequentially to $11.031 billion in its fiscal first quarter, and the company projected $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion for fiscal second quarter. The midpoint is $12.4 billion; dividing the $1.369 billion increase by the $11.031 billion starting figure gives 12.4%. The low and high ends imply growth of 10.6% and 14.2%, respectively. Sandisk's data-center revenue rose 61% sequentially to $4.802 billion, while consumer revenue declined 29% to $397 million. This mix is one reason a flat forecast at Kioxia need not invalidate Sandisk's guidance.

The shared supply chain and the unshared revenue line

The joint-venture link is the standout feature of this comparison. Sandisk and Kioxia do not merely observe the same NAND market from afar; they use common wafer ventures. But the Kioxia filing splits revenue among SSD and Storage, Smart Devices and Other, while Sandisk reports Datacenter, Edge and Consumer end markets. These categories overlap without matching. Kioxia's reported SSD and Storage line includes PC, data-center and enterprise products. Its Other line includes sales to the Sandisk group through the ventures. Sandisk can sell a different mix of finished products, on different commercial terms, into the same quarter.

The accounting calendars also differ slightly. Kioxia's forecast covers October 1 through December 31, 2026. Sandisk's guidance is for its fiscal second quarter following a quarter that ended October 2. The two outlooks largely cover the same demand window but are not perfectly aligned. Nor should operating profit margins be compared directly without reconciling IFRS, U.S. GAAP, non-GAAP adjustments and each company's venture accounting. The more defensible cross-check is sequential revenue growth within each company, then an explanation of why that growth may differ.

Kioxia's reported June-to-September revenue jump was about ¥712.9 billion, or 40.3% on the ¥1.7671 trillion starting quarter. Its October-to-December forecast adds only ¥20 billion, or 0.8%. Sandisk's prior revenue increase was $2.066 billion, or 23.0% on $8.965 billion; its guidance midpoint adds another $1.369 billion, or 12.4%. Both imply deceleration, but Kioxia's is far steeper. That difference is an early warning to test Sandisk's assumptions on selling prices, data-center mix and customer commitments when its next numbers arrive.

What the Tokyo price is actually saying

At the measured 9:34 a.m. Japan time quote, Kioxia's ¥11,985 price was ¥1,485 below Friday's ¥13,470 close. The calculation is ¥1,485 divided by ¥13,470, or 11.0%. The delayed quote is a fixed intraday snapshot; the Japanese session can move after that moment. At about the same point, Tokyo Electron, a chip-equipment supplier with a different business model, traded at ¥10,135, up 6.5% from ¥9,514. Its October 30 forecast called for fiscal-year sales growth of 51.4% and operating-income growth of 87.1%, explicitly citing AI-server investment. The 17.5-percentage-point gap between those two Japanese share moves shows how selectively investors were treating AI-linked semiconductor exposures at the open. It does not isolate the cause of either move.

Sandisk's last observed U.S. close predates this Tokyo action. Alpaca's IEX daily bars show $1,330.74 on October 29 and $1,152.04 on October 30, a 13.4% close-to-close fall on that venue. The wider U.S. market was also under pressure Friday, so attributing Sandisk's entire decline to its own outlook would go beyond the evidence. The next direct test is the U.S. cash market open on November 2, when traders can respond to the fresh Kioxia signal. No U.S. reaction is assumed before it happens. Readers can follow SNDK's TECHi quote page for the later session rather than treating Friday's close as a live Monday price.

Sandisk stock forecast for November: three testable paths

Base case: Sandisk's $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion fiscal-second-quarter revenue guide remains plausible despite Kioxia's flat outlook. The common wafer base can coexist with different end-market exposure, contract pricing and shipment timing. Under this case, the Tokyo drop raises scrutiny but does not by itself change Sandisk's reported guidance. The stock's near-term path would depend on whether U.S. investors see Kioxia as a market-wide pricing warning or a company-specific forecast shaped by currency and mix.

Upside case: The company provides evidence that data-center demand and contracted pricing protect its revenue growth even as Kioxia's company-wide sales flatten. Sandisk's 61% sequential data-center revenue growth in the reported quarter is an encouraging historical figure, but it is not proof that the same rate persists. A sustained recovery after the U.S. open, paired with later disclosure that next-quarter data-center sales and gross margin hold up, would strengthen this case. The SNDK forecast page is a useful place to compare any subsequent analyst revisions, with their dates and methods, against the company's own guidance.

Downside case: Kioxia's near-flat outlook is the first visible sign that the unusually rapid rise in NAND average selling prices is slowing across the shared production ecosystem. If Sandisk's next reported revenue approaches or misses the $12.2 billion low end, or its expected 84.5%–85.5% non-GAAP gross-margin band slips, the market would have firmer evidence that recent profitability was closer to a peak than a durable step up. The condition is observable in future results; Kioxia's share price alone does not establish it.

These are conditional scenarios, not price targets. Sandisk also announced an eight-for-one split effective later in November, according to its earnings release. A split changes the per-share quotation, not the underlying market value or the business test. The company's stated non-GAAP outlook also excludes certain stock-based compensation, so readers should compare GAAP and adjusted profitability when the next filing is available.

The evidence that would change the call

The strongest counterargument to a bearish read-through is in Kioxia's own document: it still expects demand from data centers to be strong and identifies exchange rates as a reason its next-quarter revenue and profit may be broadly flat. Sandisk's 10-Q, meanwhile, says AI-driven demand is expected to persist through calendar 2027 and describes longer-term customer agreements. Those are management expectations and contractual descriptions, not a guarantee of future sales or pricing. A sharply falling stock can be reacting to expectations that were more demanding than the published forecast, rather than to evidence of a collapsing NAND market.

For November, the most useful checks are precise. First, observe Sandisk's actual U.S. opening and closing prices on November 2, including provider, time and session; do not substitute Kioxia's percentage move. Second, watch whether Sandisk or Kioxia clarifies how much of its next-quarter growth is price, bits shipped, customer mix or foreign exchange. Third, examine whether further filings show expansion or strain in the shared manufacturing commitments. Sandisk's 10-Q says its three Flash Ventures run through 2034 and notes an $838 million equivalent share of remaining lease guarantees as of October 2. Those are real balance-sheet and capacity considerations, not a one-day trading signal.

The forecast therefore remains conditional: Sandisk's published growth guide has room to be met, but Kioxia's opening plunge makes the gap between their near-term revenue expectations the question to verify. If Sandisk sustains double-digit sequential revenue growth with strong data-center mix, the Tokyo selloff may prove a poor proxy for SNDK. If pricing or margins soften across both partners, the shared-wafer connection will look more predictive. The next U.S. session is the first chance to observe that distinction, not the final verdict.
